title: Cognitive Science in Prompt Engineering: A Human-Centered Framework for Effective Interaction with Large Language Models
abstract: Prompt engineering has emerged as an important method for shaping the behavior and outputs of large language models (LLMs). However, conventional approaches frequently emphasize linguistic instructions, technical configurations, and model performance while paying comparatively limited attention to the cognitive processes through which humans formulate objectives, communicate intentions, evaluate information, and regulate their reliance on artificial intelligence. This paper examines prompt engineering from the perspective of cognitive science, integrating theoretical insights from working memory research, cognitive load theory, metacognition, cognitive flexibility, cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, and human–computer interaction. The central argument is that effective prompt engineering should be conceptualized not merely as the optimization of textual instructions but as the design and regulation of a human–AI cognitive interaction system. Within this system, prompts function as external representations of human goals, assumptions, constraints, and evaluation criteria. Their quality depends both on how appropriately they guide model behavior and on how effectively they support human understanding, critical judgment, and intellectual autonomy. The paper proposes a Cognitive–Metacognitive Prompt Engineering Framework (CMPEF), integrating six stages: cognitive orientation, task representation, strategic delegation, output evaluation, adaptive refinement, and cognitive integration. It additionally introduces a distinction between immediate AI-assisted task performance and the preservation or development of independent human competence. The proposed framework generates testable research hypotheses concerning cognitive load, metacognitive calibration, prompt quality, cognitive flexibility, and learning transfer. Practical applications are considered in education, scientific research, professional decision-making, and AI assisted knowledge work. The paper concludes that cognitive science provides a foundation for transforming prompt engineering from an instruction-centered practice into a human-centered discipline concerned with the quality, sustainability, and epistemic reliability of human–AI collaboration

title: Exact Bayesian layers via characteristic functions
abstract: Bayesian neural networks provide principled uncertainty estimates, but training them with Monte Carlo sampling can be expensive. Sampling-free variational inference algorithms make training Bayesian neural networks feasible, but existing approaches assume a Gaussian output distribution, which can be inaccurate in applied problems. Here, we introduce CF-Prop, an uncertainty propagation method that uses characteristic functions to compute the exact output distribution of a Bayesian ReLU layer, without any sampling, even in non-Gaussian settings. Because CF-Prop propagates characteristic functions, the evidence lower bound---the objective of variational training---can be computed in closed form for a broad class of likelihoods, including the Gaussian, Poisson, and Gamma. This allows to implement an efficient resulting variational inference algorithm, CF-VI. On CIFAR-100, CF-VI achieves the lowest calibration error of any tested method, improving on the next best method by about 35%. On a heavy-tailed insurance claim dataset, CF-VI accurately captures tail uncertainty that is severely underestimated by both other sampling-free methods and Monte Carlo methods.

title: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction
abstract: Quantum computation entails robustness engineering: a noisy quantum state is measured continuously, and a classical algorithm (the decoder) must infer corrections that reliably remove the noise, fast enough to keep up. We write several published belief-propagation (BP) decoders for quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes in a Domain-Specific Language (DSL), and search over it with grammatical evolution. Written in the language, the published decoders show their parameters in plain view, allowing us to re-parameterise BP+OSD (ordered statistics decoding) and BP+LSD (localized statistics decoding) decoders with damping, before any search, making each 17.1--41.0$\times$ faster at a higher error rate, and BP+OSD-0 about 103 faster than the ldpc package's version tuned on the [[72,12,6]] bivariate-bicycle code. Evolution over the language finds decoders that improve the time-error front. One makes 23% fewer logical errors than BP+OSD-0 with damping at 0.64$\times$ its time, and decoders evolved from random code are more accurate than ldpc's tuned BP+OSD-0 at 1/31 of its time or less. Frozen at one operating point, the two fastest evolved decoders generalize well across noise levels, code sizes and round counts, staying at the time-error front. Ultimately, we demonstrate that capturing expert knowledge within a DSL creates a powerful intermediate layer---one that effectively bridges human intuition and machine-driven optimization to unlock highly efficient quantum error correction.

title: Personal AI Systems Architecture: A Human Centered Framework for Integrated Work, Learning, Research, and Creativity
abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has created new opportunities for augmenting human intellectual activity. However, the adoption of AI tools frequently remains fragmented, consisting of disconnected conversations, isolated applications, temporary workflows, and poorly integrated information repositories. Such fragmentation limits continuity, knowledge reuse, transparency, and the systematic development of human–AI collaboration. This paper introduces Personal AI Systems Architecture (PAISA), a proposed conceptual and operational framework for designing integrated personal intelligence infrastructures that support professional work, education, scientific research, creative production, and everyday cognitive activities. Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a collection of independent tools, PAISA conceptualizes personal AI as a coordinated sociotechnical system combining human goals, generative models, structured knowledge, persistent memory, workflow orchestration, external applications, evaluation mechanisms, and governance procedures. The framework specifies seven interconnected architectural layers and introduces a human controlled operational cycle encompassing task formulation, contextualization, planning, execution, verification, knowledge integration, and reflective evaluation. Particular attention is given to cognitive autonomy, metacognitive regulation, information provenance, system interoperability, data protection, and the appropriate distribution of intellectual responsibilities between humans and AI. The paper also presents an implementation methodology, domain-specific application scenarios, and a multidimensional evaluation framework. It argues that the primary objective of personal AI infrastructure should not be maximum automation but the sustainable expansion of human intellectual capabilities while preserving independent judgment, competence, and accountability. PAISA is presented as a conceptual design proposal rather than an empirically validated architecture. Its principles and evaluation criteria provide a foundation for future prototype development and systematic investigation of personal human–AI systems

title: Seer: Guiding Small Deep-Research Agents with Shared Decision Models
abstract: Deep-research agents repeatedly decide what to search, read, and verify, often using large cloud-hosted language models for action proposal. However, privacy and local control motivate running agents on users' devices, where limited memory and compute favor smaller models and complicate on-device training. Yet inference-time guidance faces three obstacles: exploring alternatives through real execution adds tool calls, prompted self-evaluation is bounded by the agent's judgment, and model-specific guidance risks repeated adaptation costs. We introduce Seer, an inference-time framework providing local guidance that separates the agent's action proposal from learned consequence prediction and value estimation. From a shared corpus of real research trajectories, we train two models: a tool-response simulator on observed call--response pairs and a value estimator on histories labeled with discounted terminal correctness. The simulator and estimator are trained offline and reused across agents without further training. Moreover, Seer executes only the selected action and adds only real tool responses to the committed history, avoiding tool calls on discarded candidates at additional inference cost. Across multiple deep-research benchmarks, Seer substantially improves agent performance for different language models. For instance, GAIA accuracy rises from 13.6% to 41.7% for Qwen3.5-4B and from 22.3% to 50.5% for Qwen3.5-9B. Furthermore, our analyses suggest that broader candidate coverage can compensate for imperfect simulation, while prediction and scoring errors limit the benefits of wider imagined search. These findings highlight the potential of reusable models for prediction and evaluation to strengthen small research agents through extra local computation without the real execution of the discarded candidates.

title: Coherent belief and opinion propagation produces more echo chambers: corrected version
abstract: The occurrence of echo chambers is a well-known phenomenon in social networks. Echo chambers are groups of agents satisfying three properties: homogeneity, i.e., sharing the same opinion, segregation, i.e., listening primarily to agents of the same group, and reinforcement, i.e., increasing opinion similarity over time. Opinion dynamics models have been used to explain how echo chambers occur through agents updating their opinions. However, social network users also exchange beliefs supporting their opinions. Here, we aim at identifying the effect of propagating beliefs together with opinions on the formation of echo chambers. For that purpose, we complement an existing opinion dynamics model with classical belief merge operations. Beliefs and opinions are also maintained coherent guided by values that agents share. We introduce measures, applying to either beliefs and opinions, to identify echo chambers based on the three properties. This model is used to simulate opinion and belief propagation with varying initial conditions and agent tolerance for different opinions/beliefs. Results confirm the occurrence of echo chambers observed in previous opinion dynamics studies in a different setting and with a stricter measure. They also demonstrate the occurrence of echo chambers with belief propagation. Finally, they show that connecting opinions to beliefs and maintaining their coherence increases the number of belief echo chambers, but that they involve a reduced number of agents.

title: Sonicium Function-Calling Series: 50 Synthetic Tool-Use Datasets for LLM Agents
abstract: Created by Hussain Billah (ORCID 0009-0009-5686-619X) · Published by Sonicium Quantum Lab Ltd. This record is the data card and catalog of the Sonicium Function-Calling Series: a collection of 50 synthetic function-calling (tool-use) datasets, one per service domain (banking, flights, hotel booking, e-commerce, healthcare appointments, smart home and more). Every record is a full tool-use episode: system prompt, available tools as JSON schemas (including distractor tools), user request, reasoning note, expected tool call with arguments, simulated tool result and final answer, plus difficulty, split and a reproducible generator seed. The series contains 50 datasets (about 3,848,300 records in total). The full data of each dataset is hosted on Kaggle; catalog.csv lists every dataset with its Kaggle URL, size and record count, and README.md is the series data card. All data was produced by deterministic, seeded Python generators written by Sonicium Quantum Lab Ltd.; no LLM was used to write the data. Released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; commercial licenses and custom datasets are available on request. Contact: Nazmul Basher (Head of Marketing & Communications), research@sonicium.ltd · collaboration@sonicium.ltd · https://soniciumquantumlab.com

title: Reasoning-Trace Analysis Using Large Language Models for Interpretable Q-Matrix Construction
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate Q-matrices for diagnostic classification models that approximate expert specifications, but evaluations have focused on the final matrices, leaving the basis of individual item-attribute assignments unexamined. This opacity limits the responsible use of AI in measurement. We propose Reasoning-Trace Analysis (RTA), a framework in which an LLM generates attribute-labeled reasoning steps through chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and these steps are analyzed to reconstruct, compare, and inspect each assignment. RTA is intended to supplement expert review and empirical validation. In a simulation study with perturbed fraction subtraction items, four LLMs recovered the required attributes and withheld attributes the items did not require. In an empirical study with 11 fraction subtraction items, responses from 536 examinees, four LLMs, up to three temperatures, and 100 replications per condition, CoT-derived Q-matrices overlapped substantially with the reference Q-matrix (mean overlap .809) but less than directly generated Q-matrices (.877), and they varied more across replications. Inspection of the traces linked disagreements to item-type coding, labeling rules, and how operations were expressed as steps. Q-matrices with similar overlap differed in fit to examinee responses. RTA provides inspectable evidence that matrix-level agreement and fit do not.

title: On the trajectories of the ID algorithm
abstract: The ID algorithm decides whether an interventional distribution can be computed from observational data and, when it can, returns a formula in which products, ratios and summations of conditional probabilities are nested inside one another. We study these formulas by following the trajectories of the calls of the algorithm, each of which ends with a tail (an alternation of lines 7 and 2) and an exit, and we derive two main results. First, line~4 and the exit lines fix the single outer summation of the output, while the tail forms everything inside it, both the inner summations and the ratios. Second, a ratio keeps a summation in its denominator only when a repetition of the tail is entangled, and a test of ancestry in the original graph decides, before any formula is computed, whether a topological order can be chosen so as to avoid it. We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

We also derive a bound on the nesting depth of the output, and show a simple ``dimensional'' count that every output has to satisfy. Together, these results constrain the form of an ID output and guide its implementation and simplification.

title: Advanced Prompt Engineering: Beyond the Basics
abstract: Prompt engineering has evolved from the construction of individual natural-language instructions into a broader discipline concerned with the systematic design, coordination, evaluation, and optimization of interactions with large language models (LLMs). While introductory prompting techniques emphasize clarity, specificity, role assignment, and contextual information, advanced prompt engineering requires a more comprehensive understanding of instruction architecture, behavioral constraints, conditional execution, example-based specification, structured outputs, model adaptation, and empirical validation. This article introduces a systematic framework for designing complex and reusable prompt systems that extend beyond conventional prompting practices. Seven interconnected dimensions are examined: complex prompt architecture, instruction hierarchy, multilayer prompt design, few-shot and example-driven specification, conditional instruction logic, structured output engineering, and model-specific optimization. The proposed approach conceptualizes a prompt not merely as a textual request but as a configurable behavioral specification embedded within a larger human–AI computational workflow. Particular attention is given to the separation of instruction authority from document structure, the distinction between semantic correctness and syntactic conformity, the management of conflicting requirements, and the evaluation of prompt reliability across different models and task conditions. An applied methodology is developed for transforming individual prompts into documented, testable, version-controlled prompt systems. The article also proposes a competency-based portfolio framework through which intermediate practitioners can demonstrate their ability to design, optimize, and evaluate advanced prompt architectures. The central argument is that effective advanced prompt engineering should be understood as a form of behavioral systems design: an iterative process in which desired model behavior is specified, operationalized, tested, monitored, and revised rather than assumed to emerge from increasingly elaborate instructions

title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $π_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR
abstract: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5x fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl.

title: FEA solver integration of a composite World Model with a Spiking Neural Network memory Block for computationally efficient modelling of defects and variabilities
abstract: Each fibre-reinforced composite structure has a unique material architecture. The manufacturing methods used and the presence of defects lead to local variations which require material-scale models that can resolve the response in real time at every location in the structure. Concurrent multi-scale schemes provide this capability, but at a prohibitive computational cost for large structures as the number of integration points and time increments scales with size. Surrogates have been studied extensively as replacements for material-scale models to mitigate these computational limitations. A surrogate must represent an arbitrary local architecture including defects, track the irreversible material state over an unknown number of increments, remain stable when driven recursively by its own predictions, and fit within the memory available at every integration point. Here, a Composites World Model based on a Multi-Modal Spiking Transformer architecture is designed to meet these requirements. The proposed architecture combines a material encoder, a Spiking Neural Network memory block that tracks the long-term internal state of the material, and transformer blocks that learn the short-term applied strain state. The system is trained in three stages: material architecture encoding, base training on short time windows, and recursive fine-tuning with scheduled sampling to suppress cumulative error drift. The trained model is disassembled at inference and coupled to a non-linear FE solver, enabling structural scale simulation of composites containing embedded defects. Benchmarks against experimental results for IM7/8552 laminates under tension, compression and transverse shear, for pristine and wrinkled composites, show that the SNN memory block successfully tracks the material internal state and results in prediction errors between 0.4% and 4.8%.

title: WHU-Road3D: A dataset and benchmark towards fine-grained road surface mapping
abstract: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.

title: Native OpenTelemetry Redaction: Diagnostic Tasks and Cross-Incident Linkage — Research Data and Code
abstract: Research data and analysis code for Diagnostic Tasks and Cross-Incident Linkage after Native OpenTelemetry Redaction. The bounded study uses 24 main incidents / 12 pairs from Astronomy Shop Cart and Jaeger HotROD: 384 requests, 5,586 raw spans, seven released-Collector configurations, 168 native processing runs, 168 isolated diagnostic runs and 84 primary attack runs. The archive retains raw and transformed views, client/backend/log references, frozen task/attack programs, input manifests, source/image bindings, qualification failures and separately labelled missingness/tie sensitivity. Two standard-library offline replays reproduce saved outputs byte for byte. Private HMAC keys are excluded. All native observations and failure strata remain unchanged; complete manuscript files and two administrative files are excluded from this data/code release. Profiles are constructed; the study has two application families, four-target assignments and one host. HotROD database backends are simulators. The results are not a general anonymity guarantee or a production re-identification estimate. Licensing: author-created data/documentation CC BY 4.0; author-created code Apache-2.0; upstream materials retain their original licenses and notices. Container images are referenced, not redistributed. Kamil Sawicki wrote the original manuscript. AI tools assisted with subsequent editorial revisions, reference checks and preparation of the deposit metadata. The numerical results are derived from the recorded experiments. This dataset record does not imply journal acceptance.

title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
abstract: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
abstract: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.

title: Cognitive Biases in Prompt Engineering: Psychological Mechanisms, Human–AI Feedback Loops, and a Framework for Bias Aware Interaction with Large Language Models
abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly conceptualized as the systematic design and refinement of instructions that guide the behavior of large language models (LLMs). However, the effectiveness and reliability of prompting depend not only on linguistic structure and technical characteristics but also on the cognitive processes of the humans who formulate, interpret, and evaluate prompts. Human reasoning is influenced by cognitive biases, including confirmation bias, anchoring, framing effects, availability bias, overconfidence, and automation bias. These mechanisms can shape the assumptions embedded in prompts, the selection of information presented to artificial intelligence, the interpretation of generated responses, and subsequent decisions about accepting or modifying outputs. This article proposes a psychologically informed conceptual framework for understanding cognitive biases throughout the prompt engineering process. It distinguishes biases originating in human cognition from prompt-induced response effects and systematic characteristics of language-model behavior. Particular attention is given to reciprocal human–AI feedback loops in which initial expectations influence prompt construction, model responses reinforce those expectations, and repeated interactions may increase perceived confidence without corresponding improvements in evidential accuracy. Building upon research in cognitive psychology, human–automation interaction, and prompt sensitivity, the article introduces Bias-Aware Prompt Engineering (BAPE) as a proposed framework for reducing epistemically undesirable bias through explicit assumption identification, alternative hypothesis generation, controlled prompt variation, independent verification, and metacognitive monitoring. Practical examples, operational indicators, and testable research hypotheses are presented. The central argument is that effective prompt engineering should be evaluated not merely by the coherence, usefulness, or persuasiveness of generated responses, but by the extent to which the interaction supports accurate reasoning, epistemic calibration, intellectual autonomy, and accountable human judgment

title: Sequential Anytime Valid Tests for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment
abstract: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-N (BoN), improve language model outputs by generating multiple candidates per prompt and selecting among them using a reward model. Much of this cost is wasted: a fixed budget is applied to every prompt, although the computation required by prompts varies widely. Adaptive methods halt once sampled answers appear settled, but their thresholds are tuned heuristics with no statistical control over early-stopping errors. We instead seek an anytime-valid stopping rule that takes an error tolerance $α$ as input and halts only once an answer is certified to hold a majority ($θ_a > 1/2$) under the generator's distribution. We aggregate candidates by final answer with a reward-weighted self-consistency (RWSC) score and treat stopping as a sequential test over the resulting clusters. Applying Wald's sequential probability ratio test to these clusters yields SPRT-RWSC, which performs well empirically, but its guarantee fails because the leading answer shifts during sampling, and the run is continuously monitored. Our main contribution, e-RWSC, replaces Wald's test with a betting supermartingale (an e-process) for every answer the policy produces, bounding the probability of ever certifying a non-dominant answer by $α$, uniformly over time and across all answers. The RWSC scores drive the bets, so they affect only how quickly a dominant answer $a^\star$ is certified, not validity; certification takes $O(\log(1/α)/d_{\mathrm{KL}}(θ_{a^\star}\|1/2))$ samples. Experiments across several language models, datasets, and reward models confirm the predicted $1/d_{\mathrm{KL}}$ scaling of cost and show that accuracy improves over baselines at substantially lower token cost.

title: Generalist Meets Specialists: An Evolving Multimodal Agent with Persistent Tool Orchestration for Traffic Scenario Understanding
abstract: Traffic scenario understanding requires combining fine-grained visual evidence with spatial and temporal reasoning. Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can use specialized perception tools, but effective collaboration faces two challenges: terminal rewards provide limited guidance for intermediate decisions and error recovery, while repeated planning adds unnecessary cost across similar tasks. Echoing the fast-slow dichotomy of human cognition, we propose StarTV-Agent, which combines policy learning with experience evolution to support adaptive reasoning when needed and efficient reuse of prior experience when possible. During training, Role-Sensitive Process Optimization (RSPO) combines process advantages with terminal advantages, while Weakness-Driven Demonstration Learning (WDL) provides validated teacher demonstrations targeting the student's weak questions. During inference, Lightweight Adaptive Workflow Reuse (LAWR) enables a fast path by selecting suitable workflows and binding task-specific arguments and resource references, while a slow ReAct-based path handles tasks without suitable workflows. We further design label-free feedback based on execution completion, workflow adoption, and cost savings to guide workflow reuse and memory updates. Across three challenging benchmarks, StarTV-Agent achieves up to 8.0% relative performance improvement, while reducing token consumption by up to 52.1%.

title: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods
abstract: The transition from fossil fuels presents significant challenges in energy management. To ensure a sustainable energy future, it is crucial to reduce energy consumption when possible and to synchronize electricity consumption and storage with the production from sources with low greenhouse gas emissions. This thesis explores a variety of energy management methods used to manage batteries, heat pumps, and other energy-related systems. The thesis presents three simulation cases alongside one real-world experiment to compare energy management done through simple rules, optimization, and machine learning methods. Furthermore, this thesis introduces TreeC, a novel machine learning-based method that learns understandable yet efficient energy management strategies, applicable to many cases. The three key contributions of this thesis can be summarized as follows: 1) The developed TreeC method demonstrates competitive performance compared to a variety of energy management approaches, such as model predictive control and reinforcement learning, across a diverse set of energy management problems. The understandability of TreeC's energy management strategies greatly improves the transparency and trustworthiness of machine learning-based energy management. 2) The real-world experiment highlights the need to validate energy management methods on actual hardware and not solely on simulations. Both TreeC and model predictive control performed worse than in simulations, due to, respectively, insufficiently representative training data and the real-time input data not being reliable enough. 3) Energy management algorithms reduce costs in electrified Belgian dwellings, particularly in poorly insulated dwellings, electric vehicle chargers, and photovoltaic installations. title: Full Rank and Stable Sampling of $\tanh$ Networks
abstract: We study the recovery of feedforward $\tanh$ networks of fixed architecture with $P$ parameters from finitely many point evaluations. First, we characterize the set of parameters where the differential of the realization map has full rank and show that it coincides with the regular parameters in the sense of Vla{č}i{ć} and B{ö}lcskei (2021). Second, we make use of this characterization to prove that almost every tuple of $2P+1$ sampling points yields uniform-norm Lipschitz stability on compact subsets of this parameter set. Third, we prove that for exact observations, projected gradient descent and projected Gauss--Newton converge locally from sufficiently close feasible initial guesses. The same evaluations also determine the realized function for arbitrary parameters and identify parameters in the characterized set up to permutations and sign changes of hidden neurons. Finally, we develop a general framework for real-analytic networks that highlights the role of full rank in stability and local reconstruction.

title: Native OpenTelemetry Redaction: Diagnostic Tasks and Cross-Incident Linkage — Research Data and Code
abstract: Research data and analysis code for Diagnostic Tasks and Cross-Incident Linkage after Native OpenTelemetry Redaction. The bounded study uses 24 main incidents / 12 pairs from Astronomy Shop Cart and Jaeger HotROD: 384 requests, 5,586 raw spans, seven released-Collector configurations, 168 native processing runs, 168 isolated diagnostic runs and 84 primary attack runs. The archive retains raw and transformed views, client/backend/log references, frozen task/attack programs, input manifests, source/image bindings, qualification failures and separately labelled missingness/tie sensitivity. Two standard-library offline replays reproduce saved outputs byte for byte. Private HMAC keys are excluded. All native observations and failure strata remain unchanged; complete manuscript files and two administrative files are excluded from this data/code release. Profiles are constructed; the study has two application families, four-target assignments and one host. HotROD database backends are simulators. The results are not a general anonymity guarantee or a production re-identification estimate. Licensing: author-created data/documentation CC BY 4.0; author-created code Apache-2.0; upstream materials retain their original licenses and notices. Container images are referenced, not redistributed. Kamil Sawicki wrote the original manuscript. AI tools assisted with subsequent editorial revisions, reference checks and preparation of the deposit metadata. The numerical results are derived from the recorded experiments. This dataset record does not imply journal acceptance.

title: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves
abstract: Random weight neural networks (RWNNs) are shallow networks whose hidden-layer parameters are randomly generated and then kept fixed, while only the output coefficients are estimated. Conditional on the sampled parameters, RWNN regression is a linear sieve problem with random approximation space. We show that such random sieves cannot remain uniformly well-conditioned as their dimension grows. For parametrized feature families satisfying polynomial covering and Lipschitz conditions, the eigenvalues of the population covariance matrix are proven to have polynomial upper bounds determined by the covering geometry of the parameter space, leading to a vanishing smallest eigenvalue. We develop approximation, estimation, and inference theory that explicitly treats the ill-conditioning. Under a $β$-Hölder source condition, we obtain both faster-than-Monte-Carlo $L^2$ approximation rates and new $L^\infty$ approximation bounds based on stratified sampling. We then derive improved consistency guarantees for ridge-regularized least squares driven by ridge effective dimension, spectral, and leverage-based stability conditions. For inference, we establish asymptotic linearity and Gaussian limits for linear functional directions while allowing the smallest eigenvalue of the population covariance matrix to vanish. Nondegeneracy is directional: we characterize it with a ridge-normalized Rayleigh quotient and extend it to smooth functionals via Riesz representation. Consistency of ridge-adjusted variance estimators is proved, yielding feasible studentized inference. Numerical experiments illustrate the deterioration of random-feature conditioning and the finite-sample behavior of the resulting estimation and inference procedures.

title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.

title: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding
abstract: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce \textbf{WeMM-Video}, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.

title: HALTT: A HAte Lexicon Through Time
abstract: Automated hate speech detection degrades over time as everyday vocabulary is weaponized into covert slurs while retaining original benign meanings (polysemy retention). Existing lexical semantic change detection (LSCD) frameworks struggle with this phenomenon due to a lack of standardized, sense-delineated diachronic resources. We propose a multi-stage framework to construct and validate a diachronic lexicon of semantically shifted hate speech terms. Filtering > 20,000 candidates, our pipeline combines historical (1770-1964) and modern (2001-2024) corpus frequency grounding, masked definition-level scoring to mitigate LLM temporal bias, and a dual-persona reasoning prompt paradigm. We release HALTT, a grounded lexicon of 19 polysemous terms with literal and derogatory senses, analyze shift typologies, and establish evaluation protocols for downstream diachronic benchmarking.

title: Multi-Agent Prompt Architecture: A Contract Based Framework for Specialized AI Agents, Task Handoffs, and Verification
abstract: The increasing complexity of tasks performed by large language models (LLMs) creates a growing need for architectures that extend beyond single-agent interactions. Although individual language models can perform diverse cognitive and operational activities, complex workflows frequently require specialized expertise, structured task decomposition, coordinated execution, independent verification, and controlled integration of results. Multi-agent architectures address these requirements by organizing several specialized artificial intelligence agents into coordinated systems. This paper introduces a conceptual and methodological framework for Multi-Agent Prompt Architecture (MAPA), defined as the systematic design of agent roles, instructional boundaries, task dependencies, communication protocols, verification mechanisms, and governance procedures within LLM-based systems. The proposed framework integrates principles of modular system design, distributed problem solving, prompt engineering, information provenance, and human oversight. It distinguishes agent specialization from simple role simulation and emphasizes explicit task contracts, controlled handoffs, structured outputs, and evidence-based validation. A reference architecture is presented comprising an intake agent, orchestrator, specialized execution agents, verification agents, an integration agent, and a human approval mechanism. The paper additionally specifies communication requirements, operational states, error-handling procedures, architectural evaluation metrics, and a practical implementation scenario. The central proposition is that the effectiveness of multi-agent systems depends not primarily on the number of participating agents, but on the quality of their coordination, the precision of their responsibilities, the reliability of information transfer, and the independence of their verification procedures. The resulting framework provides researchers, prompt engineers, AI architects, and automation developers with a systematic methodology for designing, implementing, and evaluating specialized multi-agent workflows

title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

title: Decoupled Knowledge Retrieval and Compact Memory Enable Reliable Lifelong Model Editing
abstract: Lifelong model editing requires continuously incorporating new facts into deployed large language models (LLMs) without expensive retraining or compromising existing capabilities. Memory-based editors offer an appealing solution by keeping the base parameters untouched, yet their practical use is hindered by linearly growing storage requirements and deteriorating retrieval performance as edits accumulate. To tackle these problems, we introduce BiSpace, a lifelong model editing framework that decouples memory retrieval from knowledge injection across two distinct representation spaces. BiSpace routes queries and identifies relevant edits in an external semantic space, while injecting the corresponding knowledge into the internal representation space of the LLM through sparse and storage-efficient updates. Extensive experiments show that BiSpace shrinks each entry's storage to only about 10.2% of the original and shows strong resilience to long edit sequences of up to 16K edits. On a more challenging benchmark, BiSpace further improves Overall Performance by more than 23% over existing methods. These results advance memory-based editing toward reliable long-term model maintenance at scale.

title: RAG Systems Engineering: Designing Reliable Knowledge Retrieval and Document Grounded AI Systems
abstract: The rapid expansion of personal and organizational digital information has created significant challenges for knowledge retrieval, information integration, and effective utilization of distributed document collections. Traditional document search systems primarily rely on keyword matching, file organization, and manually defined metadata. Although these approaches remain useful, they often provide insufficient support for semantically complex questions, cross-document synthesis, and contextual information retrieval. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides an architectural approach that integrates external information retrieval with the generative capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Instead of relying exclusively on knowledge encoded during model training, RAG systems retrieve relevant information from external sources and incorporate that information into the generation process. This paper proposes a structured engineering framework for developing document-grounded RAG systems capable of searching, interpreting, and synthesizing information from personal and organizational knowledge repositories. The framework encompasses document ingestion, preprocessing, semantic segmentation, embedding generation, indexing, hybrid retrieval, reranking, context construction, answer generation, source attribution, quality evaluation, access control, and continuous knowledge-base maintenance. Particular attention is devoted to the practical problem of transforming heterogeneous document collections—including PDF files, word-processing documents, spreadsheets, research materials, notes, and project archives—into searchable knowledge environments. A reference architecture and implementation methodology are presented, alongside evaluation metrics, operational requirements, and a hypothetical use case involving a personal research knowledge system. The paper argues that effective RAG engineering should be understood not simply as connecting a language model to a vector database, but as the systematic design of an information-processing infrastructure that preserves the relationship between generated conclusions and their documentary evidence. The resulting framework provides a methodological foundation for developing reliable, traceable, privacy-conscious, and maintainable document-grounded AI systems. Research Status: This article presents a conceptual and technical framework rather than original experimental findings. Its architectural recommendations should be evaluated empirically in specific implementation environments

title: Flow Matching from Non-Gaussian Sources: A Theory of Efficient Sampling
abstract: Flow matching is a versatile framework for generative modeling that transports a source distribution to a target data distribution. A key advantage is its flexibility in the choice of source distribution, such as heavy-tailed and multimodal sources. Yet finite-step sampling guarantees for non-Gaussian sources remain limited. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence theory for Euler discretization of flow matching with linear interpolation. Suppose the source distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has an everywhere positive, continuously differentiable density, finite total variance $\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}$, and an $L$-Lipschitz score. Using the population velocity field and a suitable time grid, this sampler achieves total variation error at most $\varepsilon$ in $\widetilde{O}(Ld\mathsf{TotVar}_{\mathsf{base}}/\varepsilon)$ iterations, provided the target distribution satisfies a mild second-moment condition. These assumptions cover, among many examples, source distributions such as multivariate Student's $t$ distributions with more than two degrees of freedom and finite Gaussian mixtures with shared covariance, while accommodating target distributions with neither a smooth density nor bounded support.

title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents
abstract: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user's current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant's belief about the user. Following Bourdieu's account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent's current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

title: Context Engineering & Knowledge Architecture: A Task-Aligned Framework for Designing Information Environments for Large Language Models
abstract: The effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) depends not only on their computational capabilities and internalized knowledge but also on the quality, relevance, structure, and accessibility of the information supplied during inference. As LLM-based applications become increasingly complex, prompt engineering alone is insufficient to address challenges involving extensive document collections, persistent knowledge, changing information, multi-stage reasoning, and task-specific information requirements. These challenges create a need for context engineering: the systematic design, organization, selection, and maintenance of the informational environment in which language models operate. This paper develops an integrated conceptual and methodological framework for Context Engineering and Knowledge Architecture. It examines the relationships among contextual representation, long-context management, document structuring, external memory, retrieval augmented generation (RAG), semantic search, information prioritization, and context optimization. The paper proposes the Task-Aligned Context and Knowledge Architecture (TACKA), a reference framework integrating eight functional layers: task specification, knowledge organization, memory management, information retrieval, relevance assessment, context assembly, generation and verification, and continuous optimization. It additionally introduces a task-sensitive context selection model that treats context construction as a constrained optimization problem involving relevance, authority, coverage, recency, provenance, informational redundancy, token consumption, and security requirements. A practical implementation scenario demonstrates how the proposed framework can support research-oriented knowledge systems requiring traceable evidence synthesis across heterogeneous document collections. An evaluation protocol is also presented to distinguish retrieval performance, contextual adequacy, output groundedness, operational efficiency, and security. The central argument is that effective LLM systems require more than access to large quantities of information: they require architecturally organized, task-relevant, verifiable, and dynamically maintained information environments. The proposed framework provides a foundation for designing and evaluating such environments. It is presented as a conceptual and methodological contribution requiring empirical validation rather than as an experimentally established architecture.

title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.

title: TableRoute: Capability-Aware Routing for Scalable Table Question Answering
abstract: Table question answering with large language models remains difficult to scale: tables range from compact to million-token sizes, while questions require precise grounding of columns, values, and computations. Existing methods often specialize in a fixed inference strategy, which is brittle across different table scales and model capabilities. Full-table reading is efficient for compact inputs but suffers from irrelevant context. Table reduction helps long inputs but depends on reliable evidence localization, while execution is required when tables exceed the model context window and remains sensitive to schema and value grounding errors. We propose TableRoute, a capability-aware routing framework with evidence-conditioned inference for scalable TableQA. TableRoute first generates validated question--table evidence and identifies the required operations, then routes each instance among these three strategies according to serialized table length and calibrated estimates of how reliably the base model handles these operations. The validated evidence supports the selected route by grounding columns, values, and conditions. Across WikiTQ, WTQ-L, BirdQA, and TableBench, TableRoute consistently improves accuracy through complementary routing and evidence conditioning across table scales, while reducing online token cost. Code will be made available upon publication.

title: Democratizing Cross-Project Knowledge for Transforming Water Governance and Climate Resilience: an Agentic AI Ecosystem
abstract: EU-funded projects produce extensive evidence in the form of deliverables, reports, and case studies. However, this knowledge is typically scattered across projects and document structures, making it difficult to locate relevant, contextual information when making decisions. This paper introduces an Agentic AI Ecosystem that consolidates heterogeneous project documentation into a domain-aware knowledge base and provides adaptive access through an agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline. Documents from three EU-funded projects (IMPETUS, NATALIE, and InnWater) are reconstructed into hierarchical section trees and indexed with structured metadata. Retrieval is supported by two domain-specific embedding models fine-tuned on domain data (water and climate). On top of this knowledge base, a ReAct-style controller iteratively orchestrates retrieval actions by allocating retrieval budget across domain collections and accumulating evidence until a stopping criterion is met. In a retrieval benchmark over the corpus, the proposed approach improves Mean Reciprocal Rank by 26.7% (relative) compared to a single-domain embedding baseline, indicating more consistent retrieval of relevant evidence to support cross-project knowledge synthesis and climate-resilient decision-making.

title: EgoWitness: Benchmarking Instance-Level Spatial Memory and Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams
abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.

title: Simulation-pretrained autoencoders versus PCA for compressing multimode fibre transmission matrices
abstract: Multimode optical fibres can image through a thin, flexible probe once their transmission matrix (TM) has been measured, but a TM is large and must be re-measured whenever the fibre moves. A compact model of feasible TMs would make storing and re-estimating them cheaper, so we ask how compactly TMs can be represented, and from how few measured TMs. Here we benchmark a permutation-equivariant autoencoder, pretrained on simulated fibres and adapted to measured TMs, against principal component analysis (PCA). At 62x compression, adapting the pretrained autoencoder with just two measured TMs reconstructs the TM of a 50um fibre well enough to focus light at 98% of the ideal enhancement, and it stays accurate when the TMs are shifted by 25 pixels or zoomed by 10%, which quickly degrades a linear basis. It is not, however, a better compressor: PCA is about ten times more accurate when fitted on all 163 real TMs (1.1% against 11.9% error on held-out TMs) and is already more accurate from ten. The autoencoder's value is as a prior when few or no real TMs exist: with none it reaches 29% error, against 91% for PCA fitted on the same simulation. Transfer to a different fibre is only partial. The most important extension, not yet tested, is to recover pixel-basis TMs from fewer measurements than a full TM, which would turn the pretrained prior from a compressor into a measurement-saving tool.

title: Interpretable Prototype-Conditioned Adaptation for Weather Forecasting
abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting requires distinguishing local states and their temporal evolution. However, learned patterns remain implicit in neural forecasters, making their influence difficult to interpret. Failing to distinguish local evolution can lead to similar forecasts for locations that develop differently, increasing prediction error. This motivates explicit references for distinguishing and interpreting local patterns. Prototypes provide explicit pattern references, but sample- or task-level conditioning leaves open how to adapt to distinct locations and variable groups. To deal with this problem, we design ProtoCast, which uses group-specific prototype banks to adapt local features while accounting for cross-variable dependencies. Specifically, (1) we combine each group's historical features and temporal change with forecast context from cross-variable attention for evolution-aware prototype matching. (2) Sparse mixtures of prototype-specific low-rank operators tailor corrections to each group and location. A gated attention block then exchanges the corrected features across groups before prediction. Each group's correction decomposes into explicit prototype contributions before this fusion. (3) We jointly train the forecasting network and operators from scratch and refit each group's prototypes before every training epoch. Slot tracking preserves prototype-operator associations, making each prototype's contribution to local corrections more interpretable. Experiments on GlobalForecast and TyphoonTracking show improved forecasting accuracy, while prototype deletion links local feature contributions to changes in prediction error. This work advances the development of more accurate and interpretable data-driven weather forecasting models. Project page: https://zhixuanli.github.io/projects/li2026protocast

title: Python for AI Development: Building Intelligent Applications, APIs, Data Pipelines, Integrations, and Automated Workflows
abstract: Python has become a central programming language in artificial intelligence development, supporting a broad range of activities, including data engineering, machine learning, large language model (LLM) integration, application programming interfaces (APIs), intelligent automation, and the deployment of AI-enabled services. However, creating a reliable AI application requires more than writing scripts or connecting to a model provider. It involves the systematic design of software components that manage data, computational processes, external services, security constraints, and operational performance. This article presents a comprehensive methodological framework for Python-based AI development, emphasizing the transition from isolated computational scripts to modular, maintainable, and production-oriented AI systems. The framework integrates seven interconnected domains: Python programming foundations, data processing and transformation, AI model integration, API development, external service integration, workflow automation, and software reliability engineering. Particular attention is devoted to architectural separation, data validation, asynchronous execution, error management, reproducibility, observability, and the responsible integration of generative AI capabilities. The article proposes a reference architecture for AI-enabled applications and presents practical implementation patterns involving structured data pipelines, model inference services, API endpoints, and automated information-processing workflows. A competency-based development pathway is also proposed to support developers progressing from fundamental Python programming toward independent AI application engineering. The central argument is that effective Python-based AI development should be understood not as the accumulation of individual programming techniques but as the engineering of integrated computational systems in which data, models, APIs, and automated processes cooperate under explicit operational and quality requirements.

title: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step
abstract: Current leading video generation models can synthesize highly realistic videos, while still frequently violating physical and logical constraints in multi-step reasoning and planning, even after training with large-scale reasoning data or existing diffusion RL methods. We attribute these failures to the conventional video training paradigm, which treats a solution as a fixed-length clip rather than a chain of decisions. We present ViDecide, a decision-centric framework that trains video diffusion models to predict state transitions causally and decide when to stop, with a decision-focused training schedule. We further propose Corrective Fine-tuning (CFT), which corrects failed decisions by mapping their noise to the model's own successful continuations, achieving stable improvement without policy-gradient optimization. Across abstract games, planning tasks, and a new benchmark of multi-step robot planning, ViDecide achieves an average strict success rate of 83.8%, far above 23.3% for standard fine-tuning and 67.8% for the strongest prior method, and generalizes to larger puzzles and unseen layouts. Our framework therefore unlocks greater potential for video generation models as reliable reasoners and planners in the visual world. Project page: https://kevin-thu.github.io/ViDecide.

title: TrajCal: Trajectory-Calibrated Time Schedules for Few-Step Flow Sampling
abstract: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.

title: GateTrace: Where Do Crowd Crossings Go Missing Under Occlusion?
abstract: At large events, pedestrian tracking supports entrance and passageway counts, but totals hide which crossings were missed. In a stadium study, the system recorded about four in five clearly visible crossings but fewer than one in three mostly obscured crossings. The videos lacked trajectories annotated across frames, so we turned to MOT20, which provides pedestrian trajectories and visibility. We introduce GateTrace to locate missed crossings and assess changes to counting rules. It derives reference crossings from annotations under fixed rules, matches reports by person, direction, time and position, and traces misses through saved boxes and counting decisions. With a shared detector, ByteTrack, OC-SORT and BoT-SORT recover 38.9-46.7% of low-visibility reference crossings on development sequences, versus 98.1-99.0% at high visibility. The gap recurs on two further sequences under a protocol fixed in advance. Published outputs of MOT20-tuned BASE recover 63-78% at low visibility across both sequence groups. Losses stop at different stages across systems. Across four systems and both groups, 47-79% of low-visibility misses have no nearby output linked to the person or no possible crossing in the saved tracks. Removing later checks from BASE on development sequences leaves most misses unresolved and lowers precision against the fixed reference list from about 96% to 77%. Misses also remain among sampled reference crossings that two human annotators supported after checking the videos. GateTrace shows where crossings are lost and measures the recovery and precision costs of changing later checks. We will release the code and per-crossing records.

title: LINEAGE: A Benchmark for Empirical Lineage Retrieval in AI Scientific Literature
abstract: Current research agents are moving beyond academic search toward literature synthesis and experiment planning. These workflows increasingly rely on literature retrieval systems, which serve as standalone systems or as components of research agents. However, existing scientific literature retrieval benchmarks mainly evaluate these methods using topical relevance or citation links as supervision, which cannot capture which prior methods are used for empirical comparison. To address this gap, we introduce Lineage, a benchmark for empirical lineage retrieval in AI scientific literature. An empirical lineage relation links a prior paper to a source paper that explicitly uses its method as an empirical comparison baseline. These relations form lineage graphs whose multi-hop neighborhoods provide retrieval ground truth for structural evaluation. To construct these graphs at scale, we develop Lineage-Constructor, which converts heterogeneous paper records and full-paper empirical baseline evidence into calibrated lineage graphs. Built from 121,048 papers across 17 top AI venues from 2018 to 2025, Lineage contains 3,950 graph components, 67,502 paper nodes, 164,948 lineage edges, and 80,000 multi-facet retrieval queries. Experiments with 19 representative retrieval systems show that empirical lineage retrieval remains challenging. Performance drops sharply with lineage distance, while structural metrics reveal that isolated retrieval hits often fail to recover closely connected empirical comparison neighborhoods.

title: SEEC: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Self-Supervised External-Eye Representation Learning
abstract: External-eye photography captures clinically relevant periocular anatomy at low acquisition cost, yet no large-scale standardized resource exists for evaluating self-supervised external-eye representations. We introduce a 4.35-million-image Standardized External-Eye Corpus (SEEC) derived from fourteen heterogeneous public face datasets, together with a benchmark for external-eye representation learning. For evaluation, we provide held-out evaluation distributions, landmark-annotated anatomical probe sets, and clinical disease-classification experiments spanning ptosis, thyroid eye disease, and craniofacial syndromes. We evaluate representations at two complementary levels: (a) the representation level, by assessing embedding geometry across multiple data distributions, and (b) the functional level, by assessing anatomical recovery, out-of-distribution anatomical transfer, and disease classification. Our models include ResNet-101 and ViT-B encoders pretrained using InfoNCE, VICReg, and LeJEPA objectives and compared with DINOv2 and MAE. Our results indicate that representation-level and functional-level evaluations are dissociable: broader embedding-space utilization does not consistently correspond to anatomical transfer or disease-classification performance, and no single encoder is universally optimal. Domain-specific external-eye encoders outperform DINOv2 and MAE on cross-dataset anatomical transfer despite being pretrained at substantially smaller scale, while external-eye-pretrained ViT models match or outperform these general-purpose baselines on frozen disease-classification probes. We release benchmark code, evaluation scripts, and preprocessing pipelines to reproduce SEEC at https://monkeygobah.github.io/seec-project/

title: Whose Risks Count? What 1,901 AI Incidents Reveal About Corporate Disclosures
abstract: AI systems can harm people, yet the AI actors that provide or deploy them are rarely obliged to disclose these risks. US securities regulation is an exception. Companies registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) must disclose their material risks, including those of their AI systems, in filings that carry liability for misstatement. Materiality, however, is defined by what a reasonable investor would consider important, so harms to third parties enter disclosure only insofar as they become financial risks for the company. We test whether AI harms do so by matching 9,001 AI incidents to 18,229 SEC filings of 328 AI actors by risk type. Of the 1,901 incidents with filings before and after them, half belong to a risk type that the AI actor never disclosed, and this share varies with the kind of harm. Filings disclose the risk types of 67\% of system failures but only 2\% of social system harms, and AI actors themselves report fewer than 2\% of incidents. Securities disclosure thus records the risks that AI actors face rather than the harms that people subject to AI bear. Public authorities that hold AI actors accountable for such harms could make them financially material. We release DISC, the Disclosure--Incident Securities Corpus, to support this work.
